replies.body:
Added the `using`.

To be accurate about the stakes rather than the stated reason: no handle leaks in practice. `WaitForEofAsync` returns only when standard input reaches EOF, which is the shutdown signal, so the scenario stops its server, flushes and exits within moments — the OS reclaims the handle regardless, and a scenario calls this exactly once per process. The "long-running scenarios" framing is the wrong way round, since it is the *end* of the long run that this method observes.

Worth doing anyway because it is one keyword and complicates nothing, and because this helper is shared across domains rather than owned by the HTTP scenarios. A future caller that waits for EOF without exiting immediately afterwards should not have to know that the stream was left open.

replies.body:
Added the check, and your comparison to the Java scenario is what decided it — though the two need it for different reasons.

I ran the malformed case before changing anything, since the diagnosis claim is testable. With `MOCK_SERVER_URL=not-a-url` the scenario failed with:

```
System.InvalidOperationException: An invalid request URI was provided. Either the request URI must be an absolute URI or BaseAddress must be set.
```

That names neither the variable nor the value, so someone hitting it has to read the scenario to learn which of its inputs was bad. It now fails with `MOCK_SERVER_URL must be an http:// URL: not-a-url`, matching `ArmeriaClientScenario`'s message shape.

One nuance worth recording: Armeria validates as a byproduct of work it must do anyway — it decomposes the URL to build an `h1c://authority` client. This scenario concatenates the base URL with each path and never parses it, so here the check exists purely for the failure message. The runner always injects a well-formed URL, so this is diagnosability rather than a guard against something expected to happen.

replies.body:
Fixed the wording — and you found a real gap behind it, though not the one the comment describes.

The behaviour was already right by design rather than by luck. `Respond` passes `requestBody` to exactly one place, and `RenderResponseBody` collapses the two cases deliberately with `string.IsNullOrEmpty(requestBody) ? "{}" : requestBody`. `HttpContract.Find` never sees the body at all — the lookup is by method and path — so neither the route chosen nor the body rendered can be perturbed by which spelling arrives. I left that alone; adding a null-coalescing guard would have been a moving part to satisfy a sentence.

What the comment did surface is that the *tests* all passed `null`, while the ASP.NET Core scenario reads a body stream and therefore always passes `""`. So the shape under test and the shape in use were disjoint, and the equivalence was holding without anything pinning it. Added a theory over both spellings asserting the same answer, so a future change to the rendering cannot quietly diverge them.

The docs now say a bodyless request arrives as null or empty, and why: a framework handing over a body stream reports the absent body as an empty string, one modelling it as optional reports null, and both mean the same thing here.

@@ -0,0 +1,97 @@
+# .NET conformance scenarios
+
+Everything a .NET scenario shares: the support every scenario needs whatever
+domain it measures, and the SDK the ones measuring library instrumentation
+build for themselves.
+
+```text
+scenarios/<domain>/dotnet/                   a domain's build root — the solution and its pins
+tools/dotnet/OpenTelemetry.Conformance.Scenario/      what a scenario needs before any telemetry
+tools/dotnet/OpenTelemetry.Conformance.Scenario.Sdk/  the SDK a library-instrumentation scenario owns
+tools/dotnet/src/                            `otel-conformance-dotnet`, the launcher
+tools/dotnet/tests/                          the launcher's tests
+```
+
+## A build root per domain
+
+A domain's .NET scenarios are one solution, rooted at its own
+`scenarios/<domain>/dotnet` — today only
+[`scenarios/http/dotnet`](../../scenarios/http/dotnet). It lists the projects
+here rather than restating them, so `dotnet build` at a build root is the whole
+language's build and a shared project cannot drift out of date behind a
+domain's back.
+
+What is not shared is the pins. MSBuild resolves `Directory.Packages.props` by
+walking up from each project, and `tools/` is not under any build root, so the
+projects here read [`Directory.Packages.props`](Directory.Packages.props) beside
+them while a domain's scenarios read their own. The SDK release is therefore
+pinned once for every domain, and the instrumentation releases a domain measures
+are pinned with that domain — which is the opposite direction from a Gradle
+version catalog, where a build root pins everything it includes.
+[`Directory.Build.props`](Directory.Build.props) carries the settings that are
+not versions, and a build root imports it.

Addressed in 239e44cc43e48dafe68f3506ecb065a14bb60dcf.

Analysis: Standard input is synchronous on Windows, and the EOF read lasts for the server scenario's full lifetime. A long-running task gives this blocking protocol a dedicated thread instead of retaining a shared thread-pool worker.

Upsides: Server scenarios no longer reduce thread-pool capacity while waiting for the driver to close standard input.

Downsides: Each running server scenario owns one dedicated thread until shutdown.

That framework provides the `StringContent(string, Encoding?, MediaTypeHeaderValue?)` overload. The solution builds this call successfully under the pinned SDK, so compatibility with older base class libraries is outside this project's target.

Analysis: The existing overload compiles for this project's `net10.0` target. The string overload produces the same Content-Type header from the shared constant and avoids depending on the newer typed overload, so it is a safe compatibility improvement.

Upsides: The request construction uses the broadly available overload and no longer needs the `System.Net.Http.Headers` import.

Downsides: `StringContent` parses the fixed media type string at runtime instead of receiving a pre-parsed value.
